lede: Charge flows round a circuit whenever it is switched on, and the current tells you how fast. This topic puts a number on how much charge has flowed, in coulombs, and shows what happens to the voltage when cells are joined end to end, including one put in the wrong way round.
can: Calculate charge, current or time with Q = I × t
Convert minutes or hours to seconds before substituting
Work out the voltage of cells in series, allowing for a reversed cell

md: Switch on a torch and charge flows round its circuit. The current says how fast. Know how fast and for how long, and you know how much charge has passed. Join cells end to end and their voltages add, but only if they face the same way.

md:
**Charge** is measured in **coulombs (C)**. **Current** is the charge passing a point each second, measured in **amperes (A)**: 1 A means 1 coulomb every second.
So the charge that passes is the current multiplied by the time:
**charge = current × time**, or $Q = I \times t$

stem: A lamp takes a current of 0.4 A. How much charge passes a counter on its wire in 75 s? [4]

steps.working: 0.4 A means 0.4 C passes the counter every second.
steps.decision: One ampere is one coulomb each second: that is what a current is.
Write the equation before any number: it is the first mark, and physics papers print no equations.
75 seconds, each carrying 0.4 coulombs past the counter.
The answer and its unit, coulombs, are a mark each.

prompt: A current of 2 A flows for 5 s. How much charge passes a point in the circuit, in coulombs?
explain: Multiply the current by the time, as in steps 2 to 4 of the See it: every second 2 coulombs pass the point, for 5 seconds, so Q = I × t = 2 × 5 = 10 C.

twin.prompt: A current of 6 A flows for 4 s. How much charge passes a point in the circuit, in coulombs?
twin.explain: Each second 6 coulombs pass, for 4 seconds: Q = I × t = 6 × 4 = 24 C.

md: A lamp does not use up charge. It takes **energy** from the charge passing through it, and the same coulombs flow on round the circuit and back to the cell. That is why the current is the same all the way round a single loop.

stem: Counter 1, on the wire into the lamp, and counter 2, on the wire out of it, both read 30 C after 75 s. Explain what this shows about the charge. [2]

steps.working: The same charge, 30 C, leaves the lamp as enters it.
steps.decision: Equal readings into and out of the lamp: nothing is lost on the way through.

steps.working: So the lamp does not use up charge: the coulombs flow on round the loop.
steps.decision: Used-up charge would show as counter 2 reading less than counter 1. That near-miss never happens.

steps.working: What the lamp takes from the charge is energy, given out as light and heat.
steps.decision: Energy, not charge, is what a component uses.

prompt: A lamp in a circuit lights up. What happens to the charge that flows through the lamp?
options: it carries on round the circuit and back to the cell
it is used up by the lamp
it is stored inside the lamp
answer: it carries on round the circuit and back to the cell
explain: Look at steps 2 and 3 of the See it: the counters on the wires into and out of the lamp read the same. The lamp takes energy from the charge, not the charge itself, so the charge carries on round the circuit and back to the cell.

optionNotes.option: it is used up by the lamp
optionNotes.why: The lamp glows, so it seems to consume something. It uses energy, not charge: the counter after the lamp reads as much as the one before it.

optionNotes.option: it is stored inside the lamp
optionNotes.why: Charge piling up in the lamp would make the counter after it read less. It reads the same, so nothing is stored there.

twin.prompt: A heater glows in a single loop with a cell. How does the current in the wire into the heater compare with the current in the wire out of it?
options: the two currents are the same
twin.answer: the two currents are the same
twin.explain: Charge is not used up in the heater, so as many coulombs leave it each second as enter it. The current is the same all round a single loop.

optionNotes.why: It feels as if the heater uses some of the current up. It uses energy; the charge, and so the current, carries on unchanged.
Nothing in the heater adds charge to the loop, so the current cannot grow on the way through it.

title: Why the time must be in seconds
md: Because the ampere is defined per second: one ampere is one coulomb every second. Put a time in minutes into $Q = I \times t$ and the answer comes out 60 times too small.

title: What examiners saw
md: **Summer 2025 Foundation:** in an electrical calculation, a significant minority did not convert 10 minutes into seconds and lost marks for it. The same slip was reported in Summer 2024.

stem: Change 7 minutes, and then 1.25 hours, into seconds. [2]

steps.decision: The ampere counts coulombs per second, so every time goes into seconds first.
Multiply minutes by 60, on a line of its own, before anything is substituted.
An hour is 60 × 60 = 3600 s, so multiply hours by 3600. A decimal hour needs no extra step.

prompt: A heater is switched on for 2.5 minutes. How many seconds is that?
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, multiply the minutes by 60: 2.5 × 60 = 150 s. Half a minute is 30 seconds, so the decimal is no problem once you multiply.

twin.prompt: A kettle boils in 3.5 minutes. How many seconds is that?
twin.explain: Each minute is 60 seconds, so multiply by 60: 3.5 × 60 = 210 s.

text: A time in minutes, start to finish

md: When the time is given in minutes, a charge calculation is worth [5]: the equation, the conversion, the substitution, the answer and the unit C, a mark each. Write them in that order, one line each, and the marks follow the lines.

stem: A laptop charger supplies a current of 1.6 A for 15 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows. Give the unit with your answer. [5]

steps.decision: The equation first, from memory.
Seconds before substituting: the conversion earns its own mark.
Substitute the current and the converted time.
The number and the unit, C for coulombs, are a mark each. Type your line before it is shown.

title: GCSE Physics - Charge / Current / Time (2027/28 exams)
why: Another teacher works the same equation, converting minutes to seconds first. It is made for other boards: its potential difference is CCEA's voltage, and its energy–charge–voltage equation is not on the CCEA Double Award specification.

prompt: A portable radio takes a current of 0.6 A for 5 minutes. How much charge flows, in coulombs?
explain: Follow steps 1 to 4 of the See it: Q = I × t, then the time in seconds, t = 5 × 60 = 300 s, then Q = 0.6 × 300 = 180 C. The conversion line earns a mark of its own.

twin.prompt: A games console takes a current of 0.9 A for 10 minutes. How much charge flows, in coulombs?
twin.explain: Seconds first: t = 10 × 60 = 600 s. Then Q = I × t = 0.9 × 600 = 540 C.

text: Finding the current or the time

md:
The same equation rearranges two ways:
**current = charge ÷ time**, $I = Q \div t$
**time = charge ÷ current**, $t = Q \div I$
Write the rearranged equation as your first line. A time in minutes still becomes seconds first.

stem: A charge of 1080 C flows through a motor in 6 minutes. Calculate the current. [4]

steps.decision: Current is the charge passing each second, so divide: the rearranged equation is the first line.
The time into seconds before it is used.
Substitute the charge and the time in seconds.
The current in amperes.

prompt: A charge of 64 C passes through a heater in 32 s. What is the current, in amperes?
explain: As in steps 1 and 3 of the See it, divide the charge by the time: I = Q ÷ t = 64 ÷ 32 = 2 A. The time is already in seconds, so there is nothing to convert.

twin.prompt: A charge of 200 C passes through a lamp in 50 s. What is the current, in amperes?
twin.explain: The current is the charge each second: I = Q ÷ t = 200 ÷ 50 = 4 A.

md: A **battery** is two or more cells joined **in series**, end to end. Read each cell from its symbol: the long thin plate is positive (+) and the short thick plate negative (−). Cells facing the same way **add** their voltages. A cell turned the wrong way round pushes against the others, so its voltage is **subtracted**.

steps.working: The second cell's long thin plate, its + terminal, faces the other way from the rest.
steps.decision: Polarity from the symbol: long thin plate +, short thick plate −.

steps.working: Three cells face the same way: $2.0 + 2.0 + 2.0 = 6.0$ V
steps.decision: Cells facing the same way add.

steps.working: The second cell pushes back, so its 2.0 V is subtracted.
steps.decision: A cell turned round opposes the others: it does not just stop helping.
The total voltage of the four.

prompt: Three 3 V coin cells are stacked in series. One of them has been put in upside down. What is the total voltage, in volts?
explain: As in steps 2 to 4 of the See it: the two cells facing the same way add, 3 + 3 = 6 V, and the reversed one is subtracted, 6 − 3 = 3 V. One cell turned round cancels one of the others.

twin.prompt: Four 6 V batteries are joined end to end, one of them facing the other way. What is their total voltage, in volts?
twin.explain: Three batteries facing the same way add, 6 + 6 + 6 = 18 V; the reversed one is subtracted, 18 − 6 = 12 V.

md: Two batteries joined so that they face each other push in opposite directions. Their voltages are **subtracted**, and whatever is left over drives the current, in the direction of the bigger battery. A voltmeter across both reads the difference.

stem: A 6 V battery and a 4 V battery are joined in series, facing opposite ways, with a lamp. What does a voltmeter across both batteries read, and does the lamp light? [2]

steps.working: The batteries face opposite ways, so each pushes against the other.
steps.decision: Read the polarity: positive joined to positive means the two pushes oppose.
Opposing voltages subtract: the bigger push minus the smaller.

steps.working: The lamp glows dimly: 2 V still drives a small current.
steps.decision: The 6 V battery wins, so the current flows in its direction.

task: Join two batteries end to end with a light bulb to make a loop, and put a voltmeter across the two batteries. Read it. Now reverse one battery: watch the voltmeter and the bulb. The simulation has no charge counter, so use it for the batteries only.

prompt: Two 9 V batteries are joined in series and one is turned round. What does a voltmeter across both of them read, in volts?
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, subtract the voltages of batteries facing opposite ways: 9 − 9 = 0 V. The two pushes are equal, so nothing is left to drive a current and the bulb stays off.

twin.prompt: A 12 V battery and a 9 V battery are joined in series, facing opposite ways. What does a voltmeter across both read, in volts?
twin.explain: Opposing batteries subtract: 12 − 9 = 3 V, and the current flows in the 12 V battery's direction.

md: **Boxes for + and −.** Summer 2022, 2023 and 2025 Foundation drew a cell or battery with empty boxes to mark its polarity. Put + beside the long thin plate and − beside the short thick one.
**The current is on a label.** Summer 2024 printed a drill's information plate, with its current, voltage and frequency, and asked for the charge. Take only the value in amperes.
**A huge current for a tiny time.** Summer 2021 Higher used a lightning flash. Type the time exactly as printed, decimal places and all, and the charge comes out small.

stem: A toaster's information plate reads: 230 V, 50 Hz, 920 W, 4 A. It toasts for 165 s. Calculate the charge that flows. Give the unit with your answer. [4]

steps.decision: Of the four values only the one in amperes is a current. Volts, hertz and watts are not needed for charge.
The equation first, then the current from the plate and the time, already in seconds: a mark each.
The answer and its unit, a mark each.

prompt: A kettle's information plate reads: 230 V, 50 Hz, 2760 W, 12 A. The kettle is switched on for 90 s. Which line starts the charge calculation?
explain: As in step 1 of the See it, take only the value in amperes: charge is current × time, and the current is 12 A. The volts, hertz and watts are not needed for charge, so the first line is Q = 12 × 90, which gives 1080 C.

optionNotes.why: 230 is the biggest-looking value on the plate, but it is in volts. Charge needs the current, the value in amperes.
2760 is the power in watts. Power × time is energy, not charge: charge needs the current, 12 A.

twin.prompt: A hairdryer's information plate reads: 230 V, 50 Hz, 1840 W, 8 A. It runs for 60 s. Which line starts the charge calculation?
twin.explain: Charge is current × time, and the current is the value in amperes, 8 A. So the first line is Q = 8 × 60, which gives 480 C.

optionNotes.why: 1840 is the power in watts; power × time gives energy in joules, not charge.
230 is the voltage. Charge needs the current, the value in amperes.

md:
Calculate charge with Q = I × t, and rearrange it for a current or a time.
Put a time in minutes or hours into seconds before you substitute.
Say what 1 A means: one coulomb past a point each second, all round the loop.
Add cells in series, subtracting any cell that faces the wrong way.
Take the current off an information plate; mark + at the long thin plate.

Charge is usually one part of a longer electricity question: [4] for the equation, the substitution, the answer and the unit C, or [5] when a time in minutes must be converted. The first mark is for writing Q = I × t before any number. Cells in series come with a diagram: check which way each faces before adding. Stuck? Write the equation, then the time in seconds.
